Holstein
HOLE-stine
n. (the duchy between the Elbe and Denmark where Lutheran preaching began in 1522 and by which it entered the Danish kingdom)
German Holstein, from Old Saxon Holseta, the dwellers in the wood; held with Schleswig by the Danish crown and the Gottorp dukes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Holstein is the duchy through which the Reformation entered Scandinavia. German-speaking, lying between the Elbe and the Danish border and bound to the Danish crown, it heard Lutheran preaching very early: Hermann Tast was preaching evangelically at Husum by 1522, reportedly in the churchyard when the church was closed to him, and the towns of Flensburg, Kiel and Itzehoe followed. Duke Christian, who governed Schleswig and Holstein before he became Christian III of Denmark, had been present at the Diet of Worms in 1521 and came away convinced; he established the Reformation in his duchies, and when he won the Danish civil war and the crown in 1536 he brought the same settlement to Denmark and Norway, inviting Johannes Bugenhagen from Wittenberg to draw up the church ordinance and to crown him in 1537. Holstein is therefore the hinge: a German duchy whose prince carried the Lutheran order into two kingdoms, and whose own churches were ordered on Bugenhagen's pattern of a superintendent, a catechising ministry and a school in every town. The dictionary enters Holstein because the Scandinavian Reformation is usually told as a royal act, and the preaching in a Husum churchyard came first.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority; a superintendent as one who has the oversight; a churchyard as the ground adjoining a church; and to catechise as to instruct by question and answer.

expand to see more

ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite or ceremony.

SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.

CHURCHYARD, n. The ground adjoining a church, in which the dead are buried; a cemetery.

CATECHISE, v. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.

HINGE, n. The hook or joint on which a door or gate turns; that on which any thing depends or turns.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Act 20:20 — "And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,"

Mar 16:15 — "And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature."

Act 5:42 — "And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

Duchy between the Elbe and Denmark where Hermann Tast preached evangelically from 1522, and whose duke carried the Lutheran order into Denmark and Norway in 1536.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the history that begins with the king and forgets the preacher. The Danish and Norwegian Reformations are commonly dated from Christian III's victory in 1536 and Bugenhagen's ordinance of 1537, which is true as far as the law goes; what made the duke a Lutheran was preaching he had heard, and what made Holstein ready was fifteen years of it in towns and churchyards. The command stands on the preacher before it reaches the prince: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2), and a churchyard in Husum is out of season.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary persistence of house-to-house teaching, which is what Bugenhagen's ordinance then organised across three kingdoms. The apostolic pattern is given twice: Paul taught “publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20), and the first disciples “ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42) daily in the temple and in every house. The commission that sent Tast into the churchyard is the same that sent Bugenhagen to Copenhagen, to “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; Greek didasko (G1321), to teach; Greek euangelion (G2098), the gospel.

expand to see more

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season”, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Greek eukairos (G2122) — timely, in season; “be instant in season, out of season”, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Greek didasko (G1321) — to teach, to instruct; “and have taught you publickly, and from house to house”, Acts 20:20.

Greek euangelion (G2098) — good news, the gospel; “preach the gospel to every creature”, Mark 16:15.

Greek pauo (G3973) — to cease, to leave off; “they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ”, Acts 5:42.

Usage

"“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — Hermann Tast in the Husum churchyard from 1522."

"“and have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20) — Bugenhagen's ordinance of 1537 and its town schools."

"“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — a duchy's settlement carried into two kingdoms."
